o: An edge lies on some shortest 0→(n−1) path iff it can sit on one: d0[a] + w + d1[b] = D or d0[b] + w + d1[a] = D, where d0/d1 are shortest-distance arrays from the two endpoints and D is the total shortest distance. Example 1 has D = 5 and six of eight edges satisfy this. Two Dijkstra runs (O(m log n)) plus an O(m) edge scan is the whole algorithm; the graph may be disconnected (then D = ∞ and every edge is false). An alternative view builds the shortest-path DAG (edges tightening d0) and checks reachability from both ends within it.
k: Edge (a,b,w) is on a shortest path iff d0[a]+w+d1[b] == D or d0[b]+w+d1[a] == D.
Two Dijkstra computations from node 0 and node n−1 supply all needed distances.
Equivalently: build the shortest-path DAG from d0 and test whether the edge connects a vertex reachable from 0 to one co-reachable from n−1.

a.i: Run Dijkstra from both endpoints. For each edge, plug its endpoints and weight into the equality above; either orientation proving total distance D certifies membership in some shortest path.
s: Build the adjacency list and run Dijkstra from 0 and from n−1.
For each edge (a,b,w) output d0[a]+w+d1[b] == D or d0[b]+w+d1[a] == D.
a.t: O(m log n) — two Dijkstra runs dominate; the edge scan is O(m).
a.sp: O(n + m) for adjacency and distance arrays.

a.i: From d0 alone, orient every edge (u,v,w) with d0[u] + w == d0[v] as a DAG arc. An edge is on a shortest path iff some orientation has its tail reachable from 0 and its head co-reachable from n−1 (checked with one BFS on the DAG and one on its reverse).
s: Run Dijkstra from 0; build DAG arcs for edges satisfying d0[u] + w == d0[v] (both orientations considered).
BFS from 0 on the DAG to mark reachable tails; BFS from n−1 on the reverse DAG to mark co-reachable heads.
Mark an edge true if any valid orientation pairs a reachable tail with a co-reachable head.
a.t: O(m log n) — one Dijkstra plus two linear BFS sweeps.
a.sp: O(n + m) for the DAG and visibility arrays.

w: Approach 1 is shorter and what I'd submit; approach 2 generalizes nicely (e.g., counting shortest paths or listing them). Pitfalls: 32-bit overflow when summing weights up to 1e5 over long paths (use 64-bit distances in C++/Java), infinity-plus-weight staying equal to infinity in C++ (guard with finiteness checks), and undirected edges needing BOTH orientation tests. Follow-up: count the number of shortest paths, or find edges lying on EVERY shortest path (cut edges of the DAG).
